nameStory: This moth earned the name "false hemlock looper" because its caterpillars feed on hemlock trees and move in the characteristic looping motion of inchworms, arching their backs as they crawl. The "false" part distinguishes it from the true hemlock looper, a closely related species that shares similar habits and appearance.
description: The False Hemlock Looper Moth is a small, delicate member of the geometer moth family with wings that span about an inch across. These moths have subtle gray and brown patterning that helps them blend perfectly against tree bark during the day. Like all geometers, their caterpillars are inchworms that create that familiar arching, measuring motion as they crawl along conifer needles. Adults are most active from late August through September in New England.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Forewings show a mottled gray and brown pattern with subtle wavy lines crossing the wings, creating excellent bark-like camouflage when the moth rests with wings spread flat

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small moth with wingspan of about 30mm (roughly 1.2 inches), fitting comfortably on a quarter when wings are fully spread

idTips.label: Wing Position at Rest
idTips.description: Holds wings horizontally outward from body when resting, rather than folded tent-like over the back as many other moths do

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, delicate body typical of geometers, much thinner and more fragile-looking than the robust bodies of sphinx or tiger moths

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat weak, fluttery motion and is easily attracted to artificial lights on late summer evenings

habitat: Look for these moths in coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially where hemlock, balsam fir, and spruce trees grow. They're common in both lowland forests and mountainous areas up to moderate elevations. The adults are often found resting on the bark of the same conifer trees their caterpillars feed on.

seasonality.spring: No adult moths present; eggs from the previous fall are developing and early larval stages may be present but are too small to easily spot.
seasonality.summer: Caterpillars are actively feeding on conifer needles through mid to late summer, growing larger and easier to spot as green inchworms on hemlock and fir branches.
seasonality.fall: Adult moths emerge in late August and fly through September, when they can be found at outdoor lights or resting on tree bark during daylight hours.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died after mating and laying eggs; the species overwinters as eggs that will hatch the following spring.

funFact: The caterpillars of this moth are so well-camouflaged that they can perfectly mimic conifer twigs, complete with fake bark texture and the ability to hold themselves rigid at an angle for hours, making them nearly impossible to spot even when you're looking right at them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small geometer moths, but the False Hemlock Looper's preference for coniferous trees and its specific gray-brown bark-like wing pattern help distinguish it from geometers found in deciduous forests. Remember: if you find it near hemlocks or firs in late summer, you're likely looking at the right species.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the hemlock trees these moths feed on with the poisonous hemlock plant that killed Socrates - they're completely unrelated! Hemlock trees are beautiful evergreen conifers that are actually quite beneficial to forest ecosystems and pose no danger to humans.
compareHints: Since this is the only Nepytia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small geometer moths in the region. Unlike many geometers that prefer deciduous trees, the False Hemlock Looper sticks to conifers and has more subdued gray-brown coloring compared to the often more boldly patterned geometers found on oak, maple, and birch trees.
